subChunks.title: LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, FULL OUTER JOIN
subChunks.hookHtml: INNER JOIN discards unmatched rows. Sometimes you need to keep them — with NULLs filling in the gaps. That is what outer joins do.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
LEFT JOIN — keep all left rows

SELECT a.name, m.name AS mentor
FROM   apprentices AS a
LEFT JOIN mentors AS m ON a.mentor_id = m.id;

Every apprentice appears. If an apprentice has no mentor, mentor is NULL in that row.

RIGHT JOIN — keep all right rows

SELECT a.name, m.name AS mentor
FROM   apprentices AS a
RIGHT JOIN mentors AS m ON a.mentor_id = m.id;

Every mentor appears. Mentors with no apprentices get a NULL in the name column. Rare in practice — you can always rewrite as LEFT JOIN by swapping table order.

FULL OUTER JOIN — keep all rows from both

SELECT a.name, m.name AS mentor
FROM   apprentices AS a
FULL OUTER JOIN mentors AS m ON a.mentor_id = m.id;

Unmatched apprentices and unmatched mentors both appear, each with NULLs on the missing side. Not supported in older MySQL (use UNION of LEFT + RIGHT instead).

Finding unmatched rows (anti-join pattern)

-- Apprentices with NO mentor:
SELECT a.name
FROM   apprentices AS a
LEFT JOIN mentors AS m ON a.mentor_id = m.id
WHERE  m.id IS NULL;

storyBeats.text: 'Show me ALL apprentices — even those without a mentor.' INNER JOIN won't do.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table. Unmatched rows get NULLs on the right side. The anti-join pattern — LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.id IS NULL — finds rows with no match. It is the most useful trick in the outer join toolbox.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 All apprentices, mentor optional

Return all apprentices' name and their mentor's name aliased as mentor. Apprentices without a mentor should appear with NULL in the mentor column.

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns 6 rows (all apprentices including unmentored)

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo — Anti-join

Using the anti-join pattern (LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.id IS NULL), return the name of every apprentice who has no assigned mentor.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN. Give an example of when you would need LEFT JOIN instead of INNER JOIN.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes LEFT JOIN from INNER JOIN?
options: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table even if there is no match; INNER JOIN discards unmatched rows
LEFT JOIN is faster than INNER JOIN
LEFT JOIN only returns rows from the left table
LEFT JOIN and INNER JOIN are identical
questions.answer: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table even if there is no match; INNER JOIN discards unmatched rows
questions.explanation: With LEFT JOIN, every row from the left (first) table appears in the result. If there is no matching row in the right table, the right-side columns are NULL.

questions.prompt: Using lesson data, how many rows does `apprentices LEFT JOIN mentors` return?
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table (apprentices). All 6 apprentices appear. Dorian and Fenrir have NULL in the mentor columns because they have no match.

questions.prompt: What does `LEFT JOIN mentors m ... WHERE m.id IS NULL` find?
options: Apprentices who have no matching mentor — the anti-join pattern
Rows where the join failed due to an error
All rows where mentor_id is NULL in the apprentices table
questions.answer: Apprentices who have no matching mentor — the anti-join pattern
questions.explanation: After a LEFT JOIN, rows with no right-table match have NULL in all right-table columns. Filtering WHERE m.id IS NULL isolates exactly those unmatched rows — a standard anti-join pattern.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer LEFT JOIN over INNER JOIN?
options: When you need all rows from one table regardless of whether they have a match in the other table
When performance is critical — LEFT JOIN is always faster
When the join condition involves NULL values
When joining more than two tables
questions.answer: When you need all rows from one table regardless of whether they have a match in the other table
questions.explanation: Use LEFT JOIN when the relationship is optional — when a row on the left side may have zero matching rows on the right. Classic examples: all products (including those never ordered), all users (including those who have never logged in).
